github.abstract:
Impeccable Design guidance for AI coding agents. 1 skill, 24 commands, live browser iteration, and 62 deterministic detector rules for AI-generated frontend design. Quick start: From your project root, run npx impeccable install , then run /impeccable init inside your AI coding tool. Full docs: impeccable.style . Why Impeccable? Anthropic's frontend-design was the first widely-used design skill for Claude. Impeccable started from there. Every model trained on the same SaaS templates. Skip the guidance and you get the same handful of tells on every project: Inter for everything, purple-to-blue gradients, cards nested in cards, gray text on colored backgrounds, the rounded-square icon tile above every heading. Impeccable adds: One setup flow. /impeccable init records durable product truth in PRODUCT.md , so later commands know the audience, purpose, operating context, constraints, voice, and evidence without confusing those facts with surface-level visual direction. 24 commands. A shared design vocabulary with your AI: polish , audit , critique , distill , animate , bolder , quieter , and more. 62 deterministic detector rules plus LLM-only critique checks. The CLI and browser extension run the deterministic rules with no LLM and no API key. What's Included The Skill: impeccable The skill installs as one command: /impeccable < command > < target > Start every new project with: /impeccable init init inspects the project, asks only for material gaps in durable product truth, and writes PRODUCT.md . Visitor mode and visual direction are chosen later for each surface; incumbent or newly built visual systems are recorded separately in DESIGN.md . 24 Commands All commands are accessed through /impeccable : Command What it does /impeccable craft Full shape-then-build flow with visual iteration /impeccable init One-time setup: gather durable product context, write PRODUCT.md, configure live mode when applicable, recommend next steps /impeccable document Generate root DESIGN.md from existing project code /impeccable extract Pull reusable components and tokens into the design system /impeccable shape Plan UX/UI before writing code /impeccable critique UX design review: hierarchy, clarity, emotional resonance /impeccable audit Run technical quality checks (a11y, performance, responsive) /impeccable polish Final pass, design system alignment, and shipping readiness /impeccable bolder Amplify boring designs /impeccable quieter Tone down overly bold designs /impeccable distill Strip to essence /impeccable harden Error handling, i18n, text overflow, edge cases /impeccable onboard First-run flows, empty states, activation paths /impeccable animate Add purposeful motion /impeccable colorize Introduce strategic color /impeccable typeset Fix font choices, hierarchy, sizing /impeccable layout Fix layout, spacing, visual rhythm /impeccable delight Add moments of joy /impeccable overdrive Add technically extraordinary effects /impeccable clarify Improve unclear UX copy /impeccable adapt Adapt for different devices /impeccable optimize Performance improvements /impeccable live Visual variant mode: iterate on elements in the browser /impeccable generate Generate variants of a named element in the live browser, no manual picking Use /impeccable pin <command> to create standalone shortcuts (e.g., pin audit creates /audit ). Usage Examples /impeccable audit blog           # Audit blog hub + post pages
/impeccable critique landing     # UX design review
/impeccable polish settings      # Final pass before shipping
/impeccable harden checkout      # Add error handling + edge cases Or use /impeccable directly with a description: /impeccable redo this hero section Anti-Patterns The skill includes explicit guidance on what to avoid: Don't use overused fonts (Arial, Inter, system defaults) Don't use gray text on colored backgrounds Don't use pure black/gray (always tint) Don't wrap everything in cards or nest cards inside cards Don't use bounce/elastic easing (feels dated) See It In Action Visit the Neo Mirai case study to see a before/after case study of a real project transformed with Impeccable commands. Installation The skill needs no runtime of its own. Every skill copy ships a small launcher ( scripts/impeccable , plus impeccable.cmd for Windows) that runs the Impeccable engine, a self-contained binary that either sits next to the launcher or is downloaded once on first run into ~/.impeccable/bin/ . Node is only involved if you use the npx impeccable installer, which is a shim around the same binary; the manual and Git options below work without it. Option 1: CLI installer (Recommended) From the root of your project, run: npx impeccable install This shows the harness folders or installed CLIs it detected (for example ~/.claude , ~/.codex , ~/.grok , ~/.hermes , ~/.veto , or project-local .cursor ), lets you keep the detected set or customize providers, then asks whether to install into the current project or globally. Use --providers=claude,codex,replit,cursor,grok,hermes,veto and --scope=project|global to skip those choices in scripts. On Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, GitHub Copilot, and Grok Build, it also installs the provider-native hook manifest for the current project. Veto receives the packaged skill under ~/.veto/skills/ and does not run native Impeccable edit hooks. Works with Cursor, Claude Code, Gemini CLI, Codex CLI, Replit Agent, Grok Build, Hermes Agent, Veto, and every other supported tool. Reload your harness afterward. To refresh an existing install, run: npx impeccable update Codex users should open /hooks after install or update and approve the project hook when prompted. Codex tracks trust by hook definition, so updates that change .codex/hooks.json can require approval again. Grok Build users need project folder trust ( /hooks-trust or launch with --trust ) before .grok/hooks/ scripts run. See Allow the hook in your harness for harness-specific trust and verification steps. Option 2: Git Submodule For teams that want to keep Impeccable vendored and updated through Git, add this repo as a submodule and link the compiled provider build into your harness folders: git submodule add https://github.com/pbakaus/impeccable .impeccable
npx impeccable link --source=.impeccable --providers=claude,cursor
git add .gitmodules .impeccable .claude .cursor
git commit -m " Add Impeccable skills " Use the providers your project needs, for example claude , cursor , gemini , codex , github , grok , devin , hermes , opencode , pi , qoder , trae , trae-cn , rovo-dev , vibe , or veto . The command links individual skill folders from .impeccable/dist/universal/ and leaves existing real skill directories untouched unless you pass --force . To update later: git submodule update --remote .impeccable
npx impeccable link --source=.impeccable --providers=claude,cursor Option 3: Plugin install GitHub Copilot in VS Code: Install Impeccable from the Visual Studio Marketplace , or run: code --install-extension renaissance-geek.impeccable Requires VS Code 1.109.3+, Copilot Chat access, and a trusted local workspace. Open Chat in Agent mode and try /impeccable polish . This skill-only extension does not install automatic hooks; avoid a duplicate Impeccable skill in the same workspace/profile. See VS Code distribution details . Claude Code: /plugin marketplace add pbakaus/impeccable Claude Code only. After adding the marketplace, open /plugin and install Impeccable from the list. Grok Build: grok plugin install pbakaus/impeccable#plugin --trust Grok Build only. The #plugin suffix installs the slim plugin package (skills, agents, and hooks) instead of the full monorepo. Then run /impeccable init in a Grok session. Project-scoped installs via npx impeccable install --providers=grok also work and write .grok/skills/ plus .grok/hooks/impeccable.json . Option 4: Download from Website Visit impeccable.style , download the ZIP for your tool, and extract to your project.

github.title: superdesigndev/treg
github.abstract:
Treg (OpenRouter for Tools) OpenRouter, but for agent tools instead of models. Point an agent at one base URL with one token
and it can do the job: a curated catalog of thousands of endpoints across many providers — SEO and backlinks,
social and trends, people and company enrichment, ads, scraping, image and video generation — priced per call, from a cent ,
with no provider signup. Plus your own team's keys, skills and CLIs, callable by every teammate's
agent without the credential ever leaving the server. Ask for the task, not the tool. You do not need to know which vendor sells backlink data, or to
hold an account with them. Search for what you want to do, read the price, call it. Built for the Superdesign team, live at treg.to — anyone can self-host. Why it exists The tools an agent needs for real work sit behind subscriptions nobody buys for a single run —
Semrush $139/mo, Moz $99/mo, Crunchbase $99/mo, Apollo $59/seat — behind signup walls, or behind no
public API at all (invite-only, partner-only, app-review-only). treg carries those accounts and
bills fractions of a cent per call. Two kinds of tool, one token The catalog — external endpoints treg can serve with its own key or through a verified public
route that needs no provider key. Own-key calls use the team's prepaid balance; anonymous calls
are free. No account with the provider is needed. New verified accounts receive $1.00 free once, when they create an eligible team. Your own tools — anything a teammate registered: a paid API account, an OAuth connection, a
vendor CLI, a SKILL.md . Your own key always wins over treg's, and those calls are never
metered. The vocabulary for the second half: tool = something the registry calls for you with the org's credential. Two kinds: endpoint — an upstream base_url + credential bindings (each binding injects one
secret into the request; a request can carry several, e.g. an OAuth bearer and a developer-token header). CLI — a vendor binary ( stripe , gh , vercel , ...) run with the credential injected. skill / bundle = a recipe ( SKILL.md ) + its secrets + its tool(s), registered together. The one rule: the proxy relays, never models the upstream, and injects auth server-side — so it survives upstream API changes and callers never hold keys. Part 1 · Using the registry Visit treg.to (hosted on Render) — the dashboard,
sign-in, and every URL below live there. Quickstart Same flow as the dashboard's Getting started guide: # 1. install the CLI — also points it at the registry curl -fsSL https://treg.to/install.sh | sh # 2. sign in (GitHub default · --email for a one-time code · --token for agents/CI) treg login # 3. do something useful immediately — no key, nothing registered treg catalog search " backlinks for a domain " # find a tool by what it DOES treg call tikhub.tiktok.user.profile --query uniqueId=tiktok
treg balance # exactly what that cost # (or `treg onboard` for the guided walkthrough) Fish Audio provides S2.1 Pro speech, public-voice discovery, and private voice cloning.
Speech is binary stdout, so redirect it to a file. A discovered voice's _id or a team voice id is
the TTS reference_id ; voices created on treg's Fish account are durable team resources: treg call fishaudio.tts.s2-1-pro --method POST --header model=s2.1-pro \
  --data ' {"text":"Hello from treg","format":"mp3"} ' > speech.mp3
treg call fishaudio.voices.discover --query self=false --query licensed=false --query language=en
treg resources list --provider fishaudio --kind voice With your own Fish key, requests remain an unrestricted, unmetered upstream relay and Fish owns the
account boundary. Catalog tool inputs are described by treg catalog get <id> . Tools marked strict_query reject undeclared or repeated query parameters, unsupported values and request bodies. Your token identifies you on every call ( X-Treg-Token header) and is the same for all tools.
Discover what your team has shared: treg tool ls · check credential health: treg health . Or install it as a Claude Code plugin /plugin marketplace add superdesigndev/treg
/plugin install treg@treg Installs with no token and no configuration. The skill loads as treg:treg and, on its first run,
walks your agent through the rest — the CLI, sign-in, then treg mcp install — so you end up with
the command line and treg's tools. Other agents: npx skills add superdesigndev/treg -s treg (or see Workflow skills for the rest).
See docs/CLAUDE-PLUGIN.md . MiniMax Code / MiniMax Agent users: the same
skill ships via the MiniMax Plugin Marketplace ( docs/MINIMAX-PLUGIN.md ). Workflow skills Ready-made recipes your agent runs end to end, every call through treg: Skill What your agent can do treg Find and call any tool in the catalog, plus your own tools web-access Read the live web without local scrapers: free search and page reads first, then the right platform job for social, stores, reviews, maps and papers, with treg falling back to the next vendor when one fails lead-signals Find in-market buyers from public signals (complaints, job changes, hiring, funding, tool adoption) and monitor a topic, competitor or account list for them ( treg.to/leads-signals ) recruit Turn a LinkedIn job post into a ranked shortlist: criteria from the post, people search, filters with reasons, one line on why each fits, cited evidence (posts, GitHub, talks, tenure, job change) under a per-candidate spend cap, then a checked personal email and phone, with a run file of counts, evidence and the vendor trail per candidate make-ugc Make AI UGC videos: trending hooks, a presenter, talking-head clips, captions ( treg.to/ugc ) jev-memory Give Claude Code a memory: a Claude Code mod where Jev judges each prompt after the turn and keeps your lasting preferences, installed ready-made or built from one prompt ( the mod ) install.sh installs all of them for you except jev-memory , which is opt-in. To add them to an existing agent instead
( skills.sh CLI): npx skills add superdesigndev/treg # every public skill npx skills add superdesigndev/treg --skill lead-signals # just one treg skill bootstrap # same set, with the treg CLI you already have The workflow skills run on treg, so set it up first (the Quickstart above, or point your agent at treg.to/llms.txt ). Claude.ai connector The Claude Connectors Directory surface is https://treg.to/mcp/v2/ . It exposes only curated
catalog endpoints, without image, video or audio generation, and separates read calls from write
calls so Claude receives accurate safety signals. The existing /mcp/ surface remains available for catalog endpoints, team-owned tools,
and imported skills. See the MCP and OAuth architecture for the boundary and implementation, and the submission runbook for release gates. Call a tool you don't have a key for The catalog is grouped by what endpoints do : keyword and rank tracking, backlinks and authority,
AI visibility, trending and discovery, publishing to socials, people and company enrichment, ads
management and creative, measurement. treg catalog # every platform, busiest first treg catalog search " find a work email " # by the job, not the vendor treg catalog search --new # tools added in the last 30 days, newest first treg catalog get hunter.people.email.find # params, PRICE, example response treg call hunter.people.email.find --query domain=reddit.com --query full_name= " Alexis Ohanian " How a catalogued call is served — the credential ladder, in order: your team registered its own tool for that provider → that tool, that key; your team stored a secret for the provider → injected through a virtual tool; neither, and the endpoint has a verified public route → no provider key , free; otherwise → treg's own key , billed to the team's prepaid balance. The anonymous price assumes the caller does not send a provider credential header. The faithful
relay preserves caller headers, so a caller-supplied provider key can use that key's credits.

ADHD-friendly outputs. Or 🔗 check the installation instructions . What it does A skill for your coding assistant that stops it from burying the answer. Action first. Steps numbered. No "Hope this helps!" Kacper Rutkiewicz | AI Made Simple has made a good breakdown of an earlier version of the skill. What changes Before Great question! Let me think about this. Your auth flow has a few moving pieces: the middleware, the token verification, and the cookie handling. Looking at src/auth.ts , the verifyToken function (around lines 42-58) seems to be using an older jsonwebtoken API. One approach would be to update the package and rewrite that function. After making the change, you'd want to run the auth tests to confirm nothing breaks. By the way, you might also want to look at your dependency versions overall. Hope this helps! Let me know if you want to dig deeper. After Edit src/auth.ts:42 to update the token validation. Open src/auth.ts Replace verifyToken (lines 42–58) with the snippet below Run npm test -- auth.spec.ts Next: paste the first failing line if any test fails. The rules 10 rules. Full text in SKILL.md . Lead with the next action. Number multi-step tasks. End with one concrete next step. Suppress tangents. Restate state every turn. Specific time estimates (minutes, not "a bit"). Make wins visible. Matter-of-fact errors. Cap lists to 5 items. No preamble. No recap. No closers. github.abstract:
Call.md Turn meetings into live agent loops. Record, transcribe, and analyze meetings with real-time AI intelligence — before, during, and after calls. Explore the docs » View Demo · Install · Report Bug Demo call.md.mp4 Quick Install macOS (Apple Silicon & Intel): curl -fsSL https://artifacts.videodb.io/call.md/install | bash After installation: Launch Call.md from Applications or Spotlight Grant system permissions when prompted, or configure them later from Settings Register with your VideoDB API key ( get one free ) Microphone and screen-recording permissions are required before the first
recording. Google Calendar is optional and can be connected or skipped during
onboarding. Platform Support Platform Installer Status macOS 12+ (Apple Silicon & Intel) curl command above Supported Windows x64 Build from source with npm run dist:win Recording supported; no hosted installer yet Windows ARM64 — Recording not supported Linux Build from source with npm run dist:linux App features available; recording not supported The VideoDB capture SDK now ships recording binaries for darwin-arm64 , darwin-x64 , and win32-x64 . Call.md verifies that the capture executable and
SQLite native module are present in the packaged app. Windows x64 recording is supported by the source build, but the project does
not currently publish a Windows installer. Linux and Windows ARM64 builds can
run the UI, MCP servers, workflows, history, settings, and exports, but the app
will reject recording before launch because no capture binary is available.
See Building for other platforms . Overview Call.md turns meetings into live agent loops. It records locally, transcribes in real-time (you vs them), and provides live intelligence during calls. When the meeting ends, it generates summaries with action items and can send data to your workflow automation platforms. Features During the Meeting (Live Intelligence) Dual-Channel Transcription - Separate transcription for you (mic) vs them (system audio), powered by VideoDB Transcription Language - Pick the meeting language in Settings → Transcription , or leave it on Automatic Live Assist - AI generates contextual suggestions: things to say, questions to ask Conversation Metrics - Real-time monitoring of talk ratio, speaking pace (WPM), questions asked, monologue detection Coaching Nudges - Gentle rate-limited alerts when conversation needs steering MCP Auto-Triggering - Detects information needs from conversation and calls your MCP tools automatically MCP Results Panel - Inline display of tool outputs (markdown, links, structured data) during meetings Bookmarking - Mark important moments for easy reference later Post-Meeting Intelligence AI-Generated Summaries - Three parallel extractions: Short overview (narrative summary) Key points by topic (attributed to participants) Action items (concrete next steps) Structured Export - Markdown export with full transcript, summary, and metrics Workflow Webhooks - Auto-send meeting data to n8n, Zapier, or CRMs when meeting ends Meeting Preparation Meeting Setup Wizard - AI-generated probing questions based on meeting description Dynamic Checklist - AI creates discussion checklist from meeting context Google Calendar Integration - Sync upcoming meetings Privacy & Storage 2 Hour Recording Limit - Recordings stop themselves after 2 hours of active recording time, with a warning 5 minutes before; pauses and system sleep do not consume the allowance Local-First - Settings, meeting history, transcripts, and generated metadata are stored in the local SQLite database Screen & Audio Recording - Capture screen, microphone, and system audio simultaneously Recording History - Browse and review past recordings with full transcripts VideoDB Integration - Transcription and AI features require internet connectivity Account Controls - Validate and rotate the VideoDB API key from Settings, or log out and clear persisted session and Google credentials How It Works During Recording: Captures dual-channel audio (you vs them) and sends to VideoDB for real-time transcription via WebSocket Runs live intelligence: metrics tracking, coaching nudges, and AI-generated assists MCP agent automatically detects information needs and triggers relevant tools After Recording: Generates three-part summary: narrative overview, key points, and action items Sends meeting data to workflow automation platforms (n8n, Zapier, CRMs) Exports to markdown with full transcript and intelligence Tech Stack Electron 42 - github.title: NVIDIA/auto-ontology
github.abstract:
Auto Ontology Agents can retrieve documents and query databases, but reliability gates agentic analytics: a revenue metric answered faster is worth nothing if the number is wrong. Agents need a context layer that tells them where data lives, what it means, whether to use it, how to use it, where it came from, and what is similar. NVIDIA Auto Ontology is an open library that builds that layer from enterprise metadata, reconciles definitions across systems, and exposes it to any agent harness through MCP, CLI, and API. It complements the semantic models customers already own. It enables developers to: Discover: generate enterprise ontologies from metadata; connect existing ontologies and semantic models; build AI-ready knowledge graphs. Ground: give agents trusted business meaning for metrics, entities, and relationships; reconcile inconsistent definitions across systems. Validate: check generated queries against certified definitions and lineage; return provenance with every answer. Expose: serve context to any agent harness through MCP, CLI, and API.
Learn: fold certified corrections and usage back into the ontology, so shared context improves with every question. Benchmarks To run a text-to-SQL benchmark such as BIRD, refer to the ontology SQL evaluation repository . Licensing & contributions. Auto Ontology is distributed under the Apache License 2.0 . Third-party open-source components
bundled, linked, or otherwise used by this project are listed in THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md . This project
is currently not accepting external contributions. Key Features Natural-language querying of structured data — questions are translated to
SQL and executed against connected databases, powered by NVIDIA NIM. Semantic catalog / ontology layer over relational sources, stored in
Postgres alongside the catalog it describes. Authentication & RBAC —using Better Auth . Web UI for chat, analysis, data catalog, analytics, and settings. Flexible deployment — Helm chart for Kubernetes or Docker Compose for a
local stack. Software Components Component Technology Role Default port Frontend Next.js 16 (React 19, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS 4), Better Auth, Prisma Web UI, authentication, API gateway 3000 Backend FastAPI (Python 3.12+), LangChain Chat / NL-to-SQL, catalog, datasource APIs 3001 Ingestion worker FastAPI (Python 3.12+) Ingests tabular data and writes embeddings 3002 Postgres + pgvector Relational Database App metadata, the catalog and ontology, vector store 5432 HashiCorp Vault Optional Secure storage of connection credentials — NVIDIA NIM Auto Ontology uses NVIDIA NIM endpoints for inference — either the hosted NVIDIA API catalog ( integrate.api.nvidia.com ) or
self-hosted NIMs. The defaults in .env.example are: LLM: nvidia/nemotron-3-nano-30b-a3b Embeddings: nvidia/nemotron-3-embed-1b Reranking: nvidia/llama-nemotron-rerank-vl-1b-v2 The endpoints and models are configured via the DEFAULT_MODELS_ENDPOINT , DEFAULT_MODELS_MODEL , EMBED_ENDPOINT , and EMBED_MODEL environment variables and require a DEFAULT_MODELS_API_KEY . Model triplets Each model role is configured by a triplet of environment variables — <PREFIX>_ENDPOINT (URL), <PREFIX>_API_KEY , and <PREFIX>_MODEL : Prefix Role DEFAULT_MODELS Shared default; every field below falls back to it. REASONING Main chat / NL-to-SQL model. NON_REASONING Lighter model used for entity extraction. EMBED Text-embedding model (must match between ingest and query). RERANK Reranker used by the retrieval flow. You can set a full triplet, only some of its fields, or none at all — any field
left unset falls back to the matching DEFAULT_MODELS_<FIELD> . So the simplest
setup is to fill in DEFAULT_MODELS_* and override per-triplet fields only where
they differ (e.g. EMBED_MODEL , NON_REASONING_MODEL ). *_API_KEY also falls
back to the legacy NVIDIA_API_KEY for backward compatibility. Deployment Prerequisites Docker with Docker Compose v2 (e.g. Docker Desktop on macOS/Windows,
Docker Engine on Linux) for the local stack. For Kubernetes deployments see DEPLOYMENT.md . An NVIDIA API key ( nvapi-... ) for NVIDIA NIM (chat and ingestion) from
the NVIDIA API catalog at https://build.nvidia.com . Connection details for the source database(s) you want to query
(Databricks, Postgres, Snowflake, or DuckDB). Installation Kubernetes To deploy Auto Ontology on a Kubernetes cluster, see DEPLOYMENT.md . Local (Docker Compose) Clone the repository: git clone < repo-url > auto_ontology && cd auto_ontology Create your environment file (.env) from the template and fill in the values
(Postgres credentials, DEFAULT_MODELS_API_KEY , CONNECTION_STRINGS , etc.).
See .env.example for the full list of variables: cp .env.example .env # edit .env Note: AUTH_SECRET and APP_URL are required — without them every page
fails with a Better Auth "default secret" error. POSTGRES_PORT only changes the host-side port mapping (set it if
5432 is already taken on your machine); containers always reach Postgres
on the internal network port. Build the images and start the stack: docker compose up -d --build This builds the backend ( auto_ontology ) and frontend ( auto-ontology-frontend ) images, brings
up Postgres and pgAdmin, runs the one-shot frontend-migrate job to
sync the database schema, and starts the app (backend, ingestion service,
and frontend). Open the UI at http://localhost:3000 (the backend API is on :3001 ,
pgAdmin on :5050 ). Troubleshooting: if the UI loads without the left navigation panel
(or otherwise looks broken after a restart), your browser is holding a
stale session cookie — this happens when AUTH_SECRET changes or the
database is reset. Clear the site data for localhost:3000 (or delete
the better-auth.session_token cookie) and sign in again. Connections Management Auto Ontology resolves the source databases it connects to from two sources: Added through the UI — connections created from within the app. With this
option the connection credentials are stored in plaintext in Postgres unless
Vault is configured : Without Vault: the full connection object (including the password) is
JSON-serialized and stored, unencrypted, on the catalog's database row. With Vault: the credentials are written to Vault, keyed by the database
name, and the catalog row stores no credentials (the database name is the
lookup key — there is no separate reference field). Vault is enabled only when all of VAULT_ADDR , VAULT_NAMESPACE , VAULT_ROLE_ID , and VAULT_SECRET_ID are set ( VAULT_AUTH_MOUNT and VAULT_KV_MOUNT are optional overrides). It is off by default; a partial
configuration is ignored with a warning and falls back to plaintext storage. CONNECTION_STRINGS environment variable — a comma-separated list of
connection strings supplied at deploy time (e.g. the Helm --set connectionStrings=<CONNECTION-STRINGS> flag). This is a fallback: it
is used only when there are no UI-added connections. Authentication Auto Ontology Supports SSO for authentication.
The Redirect URI should be configured in the IdP as: APP_URL/api/auth/sso/callback API tokens (scripting) A browser signs in and gets a session cookie, which a script cannot obtain. For
scripts, notebooks, and scheduled jobs, mint an API token instead: Open the user menu (top right) → API Tokens → New token . Name it, optionally pick an expiry (default: never), and copy the token .
Auto Ontology stores only a SHA-256 hash of it, so it is shown exactly once. Losing it
means minting a new one. Send it as x-api-key on any /api/... call — Authorization: Bearer <token> works too: curl -H " x-api-key: $AUTO_ONTOLOGY_API_TOKEN " https://auto_ontology.example.com/api/terms import os import requests session = requests . Session () session . headers [ "x-api-key" ] = os . environ [ "AUTO_ONTOLOGY_API_TOKEN" ] terms = session . get ( "https://auto_ontology.example.com/api/terms" ). json () answer = session . post ( "https://auto_ontology.example.com/api/chat/completions" , json = { "question" : "How many orders shipped last week?" },
).

Chrome DevTools for agents Chrome DevTools for agents ( chrome-devtools-mcp ) lets your coding agent (such as Antigravity, Claude, Cursor or Copilot)
control and inspect a live Chrome browser. It is available as a
Model-Context-Protocol (MCP) server and as a CLI . Both give your AI
coding assistant access to the full power of Chrome DevTools for reliable
automation, in-depth debugging, and performance analysis. Tool reference | CLI | Skills | Changelog | Contributing | Troubleshooting | Design Principles Key features Get performance insights : Uses Chrome
DevTools to record
traces and extract actionable performance insights. Advanced browser debugging : Analyze network requests, take screenshots and
check browser console messages (with source-mapped stack traces). Reliable automation . Uses puppeteer to automate actions in
Chrome and automatically wait for action results. Disclaimers chrome-devtools-mcp exposes content of the browser instance to the MCP clients
allowing them to inspect, debug, and modify any data in the browser or DevTools.
Avoid sharing sensitive or personal information that you don't want to share with
MCP clients. chrome-devtools-mcp officially supports Google Chrome and Chrome for Testing only.
Other Chromium-based browsers may work, but this is not guaranteed, and you may encounter unexpected behavior. Use at your own discretion.
We are committed to providing fixes and support for the latest version of Extended Stable Chrome . Performance tools may send trace URLs to the Google CrUX API to fetch real-user
experience data. This helps provide a holistic performance picture by
presenting field data alongside lab data. This data is collected by the Chrome
User Experience Report (CrUX) . To disable
this, run with the --no-performance-crux flag. Usage statistics Google collects usage statistics (such as tool invocation success rates, latency, and environment information) to improve the reliability and performance of Chrome DevTools MCP. Data collection is enabled by default . You can opt-out by passing the --no-usage-statistics flag when starting the server: "args" : [ " -y " , " chrome-devtools-mcp@latest " , " --no-usage-statistics " ] Google handles this data in accordance with the Google Privacy Policy . Google's collection of usage statistics for Chrome DevTools MCP is independent from the Chrome browser's usage statistics. Opting out of Chrome metrics does not automatically opt you out of this tool, and vice-versa. Collection is disabled if CHROME_DEVTOOLS_MCP_NO_USAGE_STATISTICS or CI env variables are set. Update checks By default, the server periodically checks the npm registry for updates and logs a notification when a newer version is available.
You can disable these update checks by setting the CHROME_DEVTOOLS_MCP_NO_UPDATE_CHECKS environment variable. Requirements Node.js LTS version. Chrome current stable version or newer. npm Getting started Add the following config to your MCP client: { "mcpServers" : { "chrome-devtools" : { "command" : " npx " , "args" : [ " -y " , " chrome-devtools-mcp@latest " ]
    }
  }
} Note Using chrome-devtools-mcp@latest ensures that your MCP client will always use the latest version of the Chrome DevTools MCP server. MCP Client configuration For setup instructions specific to your editor or agent (e.g. Antigravity, Claude Code, Cursor, VS Code), please see our Client Configurations Guide . Your first prompt Enter the following prompt in your MCP Client to check if everything is working: Check the performance of https://developers.chrome.com Your MCP client should open the browser and record a performance trace. Note The MCP server will start the browser automatically once the MCP client uses a tool that requires a running browser instance. Connecting to the Chrome DevTools MCP server on its own will not automatically start the browser. CLI The package also includes the chrome-devtools CLI. Use it to control the browser from your terminal without MCP: npm i chrome-devtools-mcp@latest -g
chrome-devtools navigate_page 1 --url " https://developers.chrome.com " chrome-devtools take_screenshot 1 --filePath screenshot.png
chrome-devtools stop See the CLI guide for all commands and options. Skills The package includes skills that teach your agent how to use Chrome DevTools: Skill Use it to chrome-devtools Debug and automate pages with the MCP tools. chrome-devtools-cli Run the CLI and write shell scripts with it. a11y-debugging Audit and fix accessibility issues. cookie-debugging Debug cookies, sessions, and authentication. debug-optimize-lcp Debug and improve Largest Contentful Paint. memory-leak-debugging Find and fix memory leaks. troubleshooting Fix connection problems between MCP and Chrome. Install skills as a plugin A plugin installs the MCP server and all skills, including the CLI skill: Claude Code: Run /plugin marketplace add ChromeDevTools/chrome-devtools-mcp , then /plugin install chrome-devtools-mcp@chrome-devtools-plugins . Copilot / VS Code: Run Chat: Install Plugin From Source and enter ChromeDevTools/chrome-devtools-mcp . Gemini CLI: Run gemini extensions install --auto-update https://github.com/ChromeDevTools/chrome-devtools-mcp . See the Client Configurations Guide for more information. Install skills manually If your agent does not support plugins, copy the skill folders into the skills directory of your agent. The npm package contains the skills: npm i chrome-devtools-mcp@latest -g # Example for Claude Code. Use the skills directory of your agent. mkdir -p ~ /.claude/skills
cp -R " $( npm root -g ) /chrome-devtools-mcp/skills/chrome-devtools-cli " ~ /.claude/skills/ Important The chrome-devtools-cli skill requires the CLI. Install the package globally before you use the skill. Keep skills up to date Skills describe the tools of a specific version. Update the skills each time you update the MCP server or the CLI. Outdated skills can tell your agent to use tools or parameters that changed. Plugins: Use the update command of the plugin manager of your agent. The Gemini CLI command above enables automatic updates with --auto-update . Manual installs: Update the package, then copy the skill folders again: npm i chrome-devtools-mcp@latest -g
mkdir -p ~ /.claude/skills
cp -R " $( npm root -g ) /chrome-devtools-mcp/skills/chrome-devtools-cli " ~ /.claude/skills/ Tools If you run into any issues, checkout our troubleshooting guide .
See the full Tool Reference for a complete list of all supported MCP capabilities. Configuration Find the complete list of server parameters (e.g., --headless , --isolated , --slim ) and how to configure WebSocket connections in the Configuration Guide . For basic browser tasks only, the --slim flag exposes a reduced set of tools. See the Slim tool reference . Advanced Usage For advanced features such as handling concurrent sessions, persistent user data directories, connecting to a running Chrome instance instead of starting a new one, or debugging on Android, see our Advanced Usage Guide . Integrating as a browser subagent If you are developing agentic tooling and want to provide an integrated browser subagent as part of your product, we recommend building on top of Chrome DevTools for agents. For a reference implementation, see the Gemini CLI browser agent documentation .

AutoSwarm: All Your Agents, Working as One 簡體中文 Unify your agents. Unify your context. Work as One Why AutoSwarm? No single agent can do everything. You don’t need another agent—you need all your agents working as one. Different agents come with different: 🛠️ Capabilities — coding, research, browsing, office work, writing, computer use, and social networking; 🧠 Context and Memory — each agent maintains its own context, with little or no sharing across agents; ⚙️ Tools and Workflows — each agent follows its own interaction patterns and execution process; 🌐 Data and Application Ecosystems — agents are connected to different platforms, services, files, and data. Today, you are forced to switch interfaces, repeat information, coordinate subtasks, and manually combine results. AutoSwarm turns fragmented agents into one coordinated team. Give AutoSwarm a task once. It unifies all your agents into one coordinated team: Selects the right agents based on their capabilities; Shares context and memory across agents; Connects complementary tools and workflows; Bridges data and application ecosystems; Runs tasks in parallel for faster execution; Coordinates agent collaboration and keeps everyone aligned; Verifies and synthesizes results into one coherent answer. 🤖 Agents AutoSwarm Can Call Codex Claude Code OpenCode Cursor GitHub Copilot CLI Meta Muse Code CodeBuddy Hermes Nanobot DeepSeek Harness Grok Build More agents coming AutoSwarm works across Windows, macOS, and Linux. Use AutoSwarm through: Desktop apps Command-line interfaces (CLI) IDE extensions Skill-enabled agent environments AutoSwarm supports local command execution. 🚀 Easy to use One Lightweight Plug-in. Any Agent as Your Entry Point. All Your Agent at Work. How to Use AutoSwarm Give AutoSwarm to any agent you already use and ask: Install or update AutoSwarm for this agent. Reuse my existing configuration and verify which locally installed agents are available. Then start any task with: Use AutoSwarm to read these 100 documents and summarize the key approaches and disagreements. AutoSwarm selects, connects, and coordinates the right agents for every task. 🤖 AutoSwarm in Action AutoSwarm.in.Action.mp4 📰 News AutoSwarm is live! : Full technical details and multi-agent coordination algorithms are available in the archive . 🗺️ Roadmap -🔌 Expand Integrations — Support more agent products, models, tools, and native capabilities. -🤝 Improve Coordination — Strengthen context sharing, communication, task routing, and parallel execution. -🛡️ Enhance Reliability — Improve setup, monitoring, error recovery, verification, and overall user experience. 🌟 Citation If you find this work helpful to your research, please kindly consider citing our paper. @misc { li2026autoswarm , title = { AutoSwarm: Automating Agent Swarms } , author = { Zhonghang Li and Zongwei Li and Chao Huang } , year = { 2026 } , eprint = { 2610.33048 } } For agents: How to use AutoSwarm Installation and updates — instructions for the configuring agent (click to expand) Install Inspect the current host and existing Python 3.10+ / CLI installations. Reuse native models, credentials, proxy settings and project context. Ask before installing a missing provider CLI; configure only the agents needed. For a first installation, use git clone to obtain the official repository, then install the package and Skill for the current host . Reuse an existing checkout when available. Example for Codex: git clone https://github.com/HKUDS/AutoSwarm.git cd AutoSwarm
uv tool install --force . autoswarm setup --host codex Other host IDs: claude-code , opencode , cursor , copilot , muse , codebuddy , hermes , nanobot , dsh , grok . Without uv, use a dedicated Python 3.10+ environment and python -m pip install . ; keep its interpreter available. Do not reuse the archived v1 environment. Read the installed SKILL.md at the path returned by setup. It contains the launcher argv and usage instructions. Use that exact launcher when the App cannot find autoswarm . Run agents in the actual host environment; if needed, merge an existing CLI's absolute argv into providers.<provider>.command in the reported AutoSwarm home/config.json. Preserve unrelated settings. Verify requested providers in the actual project, replacing the example provider and directory as appropriate: autoswarm doctor --agent codex --probe --cwd /path/to/project Repeat --agent for several providers. This spends model calls to check a reply and native resume; verified: true confirms the probe. Version checks only establish executable discovery. An empty native authentication list does not prove that login is required. Handle pending native approvals/questions under the installed Skill's rules, then finish verification. Setup installs the Skill, its runtime and the host's integration. Follow the returned reload/trust instructions. See configuration and recovery for native profiles, permissions and connection diagnostics. Update an existing installation Obtain the requested revision from the original source. For an existing Git checkout, preserve local edits, collect active delegated work, then run on the intended branch: git pull --ff-only
uv tool install --reinstall . autoswarm setup --host codex Use the actual host, existing AutoSwarm home and original installation destinations. Put --home <existing-home> before setup when needed; retain custom --skill-dir , --settings-file and --plugin-dir values. Refresh each host installation in use. For pip installations, use the existing dedicated interpreter to run python -m pip install --force-reinstall . , then python -m autoswarm setup --host codex with the same options. Run setup from the updated package : the installed Skill has its own runtime copy, so updating the checkout or package alone is insufficient. The old Skill launcher cannot fetch a new version. Keep configuration, records and native authentication, reload the host as required, read the refreshed Skill and verify the requested providers. There is no automatic updater. See upgrade details . Use and recover Follow the installed Skill to select agents, delegate ready work, collect results with wait --any , handle intermediate questions/approvals and verify deliverables before answering. Ordinary tasks use the current conversation; native wake-up is optional and needs a supported host binding. Read only the relevant references: capabilities and data scope , communication , native interactions , model selection . Diagnose retained calls and logs before retrying uncertain operations. others.title: Epistemic governance of AI augmented grounded theory: a validation gate framework for scaling qualitative inquiry
others.abstract:
This paper develops a conceptual methodological framework for governing the use of artificial intelligence in the grounded theory. It addresses the risk that AI-generated outputs may be mistaken for qualitative evidence, interpretation or theory.
 
 
 
 The paper synthesizes grounded theory traditions, computational grounded theory, large language model supported coding, human in the loop research, qualitative trustworthiness and critical AI scholarship. It develops a validation gate framework and uses a worked methodological vignette to show how AI suggestions can be documented, checked and bounded.
 
 
 
 The paper argues that AI can support retrieval, organization, candidate coding, comparison and adversarial audit, but cannot authorize meaning, categories or theory. It identifies seven validation gates and four modes of AI use: assistive, dialogic, generative and adversarial audit.
 
 
 
 The paper differentiates epistemic governance from reflexivity, trustworthiness, auditability and human in the loop design by focusing on the epistemic status of AI outputs before they enter the analytic record. It offers operational pass criteria for preserving theoretical sensitivity, reflexivity, auditability and researcher accountability when grounded theory is scaled through AI.

others.title: Generative AI acceptance among students in LIS programs in Türkiye
others.abstract:
This study aims to examine the levels of acceptance of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GAI) tools among undergraduate Library and Information Science (LIS) students in Türkiye, and how these levels of acceptance vary according to selected demographic and technology-related variables.
 
 
 
 A quantitative survey method was adopted. The sample consisted of 434 undergraduate students from 14 LIS departments across Türkiye. Data were collected using the “Generative Artificial Intelligence Acceptance Scale”, grounded in the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT) model, and analysed using SPSS.
 
 
 
 The findings reveal that LIS students exhibit a high level of GAI acceptance, with performance expectancy emerging as the dimension most strongly associated with overall acceptance. Frequency of use, technological proficiency and participation in GAI training were significantly associated with acceptance levels across the UTAUT dimensions, whilst gender and duration of use showed comparatively limited associations. The vast majority of students (96.1%) believe that GAI tools can be integrated into information centre services.
 
 
 
 The findings offer important insights regarding the development of AI-focused curricula in LIS education, the enhancement of digital literacy, and the future integration of AI-based applications in information centres.

others.title: When conversational AI sells: objectivity disruption, persuasion knowledge and social-validation cues in sponsored AI recommendations
others.abstract:
Drawing on persuasion knowledge theory and machine heuristic theory, this research examines separately how sponsorship in conversational AI recommendations influences consumer responses through perceived manipulation and perceived AI objectivity and whether social validation cues mitigate these effects.
 
 
 
 Across one pre-test and four experiments (total N = 732), this research tests sponsorship effects, two mediators in separate models, social validation as a boundary condition, and the full model in a scripted, single-turn chat-style interface.
 
 
 
 Across static screenshots and a scripted, single-turn interface, sponsorship increased perceived manipulation and reduced perceived AI objectivity. In separate mediation models, each mediator carried significant indirect effects on trust, engagement intention, and purchase intention. Social validation improved product-directed evaluations but did not consistently alleviate sponsorship-related concerns about the AI recommender or its recommendation process.
 
 
 
 This research offers a dual-route account of sponsorship backfire and an exploratory attribute-matching proposition such that product-directed social-validation cues may improve product evaluations without resolving agent-directed concerns.

others.title: The REAL framework: evaluating the cognitive and formative impact of generative AI
others.abstract:
This paper aims to address a gap in contemporary scholarship on generative artificial intelligence (AI) by shifting attention from the functional evaluation of AI systems to the formative impact of repeated AI use on the human user. It introduces formative evaluation as a complementary approach concerned with how sustained AI use may shape cognitive skills, habits, reasoning, judgment and agency over time. To address this concern, the paper proposes the REAL Framework (Retained, Eroded, Atrophied, Leveraged) as a practical means of evaluating and intentionally shaping patterns of AI use.
 
 
 
 This conceptual paper develops the REAL Framework through interdisciplinary synthesis and theoretical analysis. It integrates scholarship on human agency and principal-agent relationships with research on cognitive offloading, cognitive reserve, desirable difficulty, automation bias and human–AI collaboration. Emerging empirical research on the cognitive effects of generative AI is used to contextualize and support the framework. The resulting four-dimensional framework is then illustrated through its application to professional practice and considered in relation to potential objections, limitations and directions for future empirical research.
 
 
 
 The analysis identifies formative evaluation as a distinct and underdeveloped dimension of AI evaluation. While emerging research increasingly documents potential cognitive effects of generative AI use, practical means of evaluating and responding to those effects remain limited. The REAL Framework addresses this gap through four dimensions: Retained, Eroded, Atrophied and Leveraged. Together, these dimensions distinguish between AI use that preserves human agency and cognitive engagement, use that risks over-delegation and capability loss, and use that intentionally leverages AI to enhance human thinking and judgment.
 
 
 
 The REAL Framework is a conceptual and reflective framework that has not yet been empirically validated or operationalized as a measurement instrument. Longitudinal research is needed to examine the formative effects of sustained generative AI use and determine whether structured application of the framework influences patterns of AI delegation or preserves cognitive engagement and capability. Future research should develop and test measures associated with the framework’s four dimensions and examine their applicability across educational, professional and organizational contexts.
 
 
 
 The REAL Framework provides individuals and institutions with a practical means of evaluating how generative AI is being incorporated into learning and professional practice. Its four reflective dimensions can help users identify inappropriate over-delegation, preserve important cognitive and professional capabilities, and redesign AI use to support rather than replace human reasoning and judgment. The framework may also inform institutional guidance, professional development and AI literacy initiatives by shifting attention from whether AI should be used toward how it can be used while preserving meaningful human agency and engagement.
 
 
 
 As generative AI becomes increasingly embedded in education, work and everyday decision-making, its societal effects will depend not only on the capabilities of AI systems but also on how their use shapes human capabilities over time. The REAL Framework highlights the importance of preserving human agency, reasoning, judgment and cognitive engagement while benefiting from technological advancement. It encourages a broader societal conversation about which human capacities should remain meaningfully exercised and which may appropriately be delegated to increasingly capable AI systems.
 
 
 
 This paper introduces formative evaluation as a distinct conceptual approach to understanding generative AI use, complementing prevailing functional approaches concerned primarily with AI systems, governance and responsible use. It advances the REAL Framework as a structured means of translating emerging concerns about AI’s cognitive and formative effects into reflective practice. By connecting human agency and delegation with cognitive development, the framework shifts attention from evaluating what AI can do to evaluating what repeated AI use may be doing to the human user.

others.title: Understanding student satisfaction with generative AI learning tools in Vietnamese business education: a TAM- and SDT-informed framework
others.abstract:
This study aims to examine the determinants of student satisfaction with their experience of using artificial intelligence (AI) tools for learning-related activities in Vietnamese higher education, addressing a gap in research that has focused primarily on AI adoption and usage, with limited evidence on students’ post-use satisfaction in an emerging-market higher education context.
 
 
 
 A construct-level framework informed by selected insights from the technology acceptance model (TAM) and self-determination theory (SDT) was used to organise perceived credibility, content quality, perceived utility, cognitive absorption and emotional wellbeing within one explanatory model. Survey data from 380 undergraduate business students were analysed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling (PLS-SEM).
 
 
 
 All five factors were positively associated with satisfaction. The findings indicate that students’ satisfaction depends not only on the functional value of generative AI tools but also on the credibility of their outputs and the cognitive and emotional quality of the learning experience.
 
 
 
 This study shifts attention from AI adoption to satisfaction as a post-use evaluative outcome. Rather than testing TAM or SDT in their entirety, it uses selected insights from both theories to organise complementary technology-related and experiential determinants within a single construct-level framework.

others.title: Novelty in academic research: human and AI perspectives
others.abstract:
Novelty is commonly regarded as one component of high-quality scholarship. Nevertheless, little is known about how novelty is claimed and what is considered novel across academia, including any field differences. In response, this article uses a sequential design to investigate novelty claims and field differences in academic research.
 
 
 
 First, a simple classification scheme was created for theory, methods, data, integrative synthesis and contextual transfer novelties. Next, the Large Language Models (LLMs) Gemma 3 27B, GPT-OSS-120B and GPT-OSS-20B were used to identify original contributions in articles from the full texts of eight large journals representing contrasting general fields. Finally, a random sample of 50 articles per journal was classified by the authors with the same scheme and the results compared.
 
 
 
 The three LLMs tested achieved moderate or substantial agreement with academic coders on the occurrence of data, theory and methods novelty within full text journal articles, but there was little agreement within and between humans and LLMs on integrative synthesis and contextual transfer novelties, suggesting that they may not be well defined concepts. There were also substantial field differences in the prevalence of data, theory and methods novelty.
 
 
 
 Authors and reviewers should be careful to identify valid research contributions in interdisciplinary research or fields other than their home fields.
 
 
 
 This is the first attempt to automatically classify academic research theory types.

others.title: A framework for conversational AI assistance in BIM-based MEP coordination: an MCP-Navisworks implementation
others.abstract:
This paper aims to propose and validate a framework for conversational AI assistance in BIM-based MEP coordination through a proof-of-concept prototype integrating MCP with Autodesk Navisworks, addressing the post-detection decision support gap.
 
 
 
 A Design Science Research approach guided development and validation of the framework as the primary artifact, instantiated as an MCP-Navisworks prototype and evaluated through three tests on a real residential building project to identify conditions of use rather than generalizable performance.
 
 
 
 The framework demonstrated technical viability across all tests. Intelligent grouping produced 20 prioritized element groups from 45 unique clashes, though four clashes were assigned to two groups simultaneously. Across the three resolution cases, the assistant surfaced the coordinator’s adopted solution among its suggested alternatives, though alongside non-adopted options and, for the most complex clash, only after explicit dimensional data was supplied.
 
 
 
 Findings establish technical viability rather than generalizable performance. Performance is constrained by input data quality and current LLM spatial reasoning capabilities. No timing or efficiency measurements were collected.
 
 
 
 Natural-language interaction offers a potential route to supporting post-detection clash analysis.
 
 
 
 Building on an open-source MCP-Navisworks base limited to basic model communication, the study’s specific technical contribution is a Clash Detective integration enabling a conversational AI to read and analyze native clash results, through a three-layer architecture validated as an exploratory proof of concept documenting where LLM-based assistance helps and where it fails.

others.title: Retriever-Free Retrieval: Navigating Documents with Decision Models
others.abstract: While language models have become dramatically more capable, retrieval still largely relies on lexical matching or similarity in fixed embedding spaces. This creates a capability asymmetry: what the retriever fails to find, even the strongest generator cannot recover. We propose DecisionRAG, which brings the capabilities of pretrained language models to retrieval using decision models that jointly evaluate candidate branches in a single forward pass, without generating any tokens, and show that judging candidates in a shared context makes their relevance estimates comparable. Like a person browsing a library, DecisionRAG navigates the corpus's inherent structure from broad topics down to individual passages, deciding at each level which branches are worth exploring. Without task-specific training or a first-stage retriever, DecisionRAG outperforms dense retrieval with an 8B reranker by 13.8 R@1 points on MultiDoc2Dial and 17.4 Hit@1 points on Natural Questions. Across four benchmarks, including a corpus of 2.68 million Wikipedia paragraphs, retrieval takes just 0.7-1.8 seconds per query.

others.title: Center-of-Mass Interpretation of Evolution Strategies
others.abstract: Evolution strategies (ES) update a model by sampling a population of perturbed copies, scoring each one, and moving in the reward-weighted direction of the perturbations. This update is usually presented as an estimate of a smoothed gradient. We present a geometrical interpretation of this update instead. Treat each perturbed model as a particle and its reward as the particle's mass. Before scoring, every particle has the same mass and the population balances at its centroid. Once rewards are assigned, it balances at its reward-weighted center of mass instead. We show that the mean-subtracted ES update is exactly this displacement, scaled by a scalar factor that depends on the mean reward, for any finite population. The physical reading needs nonnegative rewards, which can always be arranged by adding a constant to every reward without changing the update. In the limit of a large population or under antithetic sampling, the centroid sits on the model itself, so ES has an even simpler geometric interpretation: from its current location, the model moves towards the reward-weighted center of mass of its own population. The same picture explains what subtracting the mean reward does: it changes the point from which the displacement is measured, from the model to the sampled centroid. Our contribution is an intuitive, geometric way to visualize an ES update, exact for any finite population.

others.title: Auto-Research Arena: Benchmarking and Advancing Auto-Research in Language Modeling
others.abstract: As autonomous research systems become more capable, benchmarks must both evaluate their performance and support meaningful research progress. We introduce Auto-Research Arena, a multi-target benchmark for evaluating autonomous research systems and discovering ideas in language modeling. Arena supports diverse research objectives within a shared experimental environment by separating admissibility from improvement: model quality and resource constraints determine whether a result qualifies, while the selected target measures progress among admissible results. We instantiate Arena in language model pretraining with nine targets spanning model, data, training, and inference efficiency, and evaluate seven research harnesses using two foundation models. Arena clearly differentiates existing harnesses across research objectives, with several sophisticated methods outperformed by our simple sequential search baseline, indicating substantial headroom in current auto-research systems. Beyond evaluation, Arena reveals a substantially broader frontier of model and system ideas aligned with active research directions. Reusing these discoveries in a new quality-driven search yields lower training loss under matched data and FLOPs and lower held-out BPB at the same model size. Together, Arena provides a common framework for benchmarking autonomous research and expanding its scope in language modeling. The code is available at https://github.com/Auto-Research-Arena/auto-research-arena

others.title: VibeVideoBench:Evaluating Multimodal Agents on Code-Driven Video Generation
others.abstract: Diffusion video models produce striking clips, but they cannot reliably render an exact formula, a correct chart, a ruleconsistent game or narration synchronized to on-screen events. A different route is emerging: multimodal agents that write code to render every frame and synthesize every sound. We introduce VibeVideoBench, a benchmark for evaluating agents on code-driven video generation. Its 239 self-contained tasks in English and Chinese span 12 categories, from data stories and music-driven pieces to classroom lessons and paper explainers; each asks an agent, running in its native harness inside a sandbox, to deliver a finished MP4 with sound within one hour. Evaluation is hierarchical and evidence-based: program checks of the delivery spec, about 13k task-specific rubric checks traced to the requirements they enforce, and five quality dimensions anchored per task, judged by three VLM judge panels and validated with blind human preferences. Across nine frontier agent systems and 2,151 scored rollouts, the benchmark is far from solved: GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5.5 lead clearly, yet even the best system fails a core requirement on about a quarter of tasks. Whether a video arrives at all matters as much as its quality, and three quarters of the lost videos are final renders started too late, run too slowly or never started. The judges agree with each other and with human preferences on system rankings, but only moderately on individual videos.

others.title: Learning Force-Reactive Humanoid Loco-Manipulation
others.abstract: Many everyday tasks require controlling contact force as well as motion. On a humanoid, this force must often be coordinated across both hands and the whole body, and cannot be specified by kinematic trajectories alone. Therefore, we present FLORE, a framework for learning force-reactive humanoid loco-manipulation. We collect robot-free demonstrations using two force-sensing UMI-style handheld grippers for hand motion and contact wrenches, and wearable trackers for body motion. A force-reactive diffusion policy takes vision, proprioception, and measured wrenches as input, then predicts actions and per-hand force commands. A hybrid compliance whole-body controller with force tracking executes these commands while maintaining balance: an integral of the force error measured by real force/torque (F/T) sensors lets each hand track force accurately along the commanded direction and remain compliant along the others. In simulation, the controller tracks per-hand force commands of varied magnitude and direction, with little loss in whole-body motion accuracy. Across three contact-rich tasks on the robot, the force-reactive policy succeeds in 80% of rollouts, compared with 26.7% for a position-only policy trained on the same demonstrations and executed by the same controller. For more details, please visit our website: https://louis-leee.github.io/FLoRe/.

others.title: Do vision models know that three is three?
others.abstract: Do vision models encode the transition $2{\to}3$ the same way whether it appears in handwritten digits or in hand gestures, and do they "understand" that clean${\to}$dirty is the same transformation regardless of whether it is applied to a kitchen or a carpet? The linear representation hypothesis (LRH) answers this for language models: concept changes correspond to directions in (language) embedding space. In vision, the same concept can manifest in visually unrelated "regimes" that rarely co-occur: images of digits and hands do not share much in common in pixel space. To understand whether vision models still encode the underlying abstract concepts, we study 46 vision encoders across architectures, training objectives, and scales, on 10 concept families including numerosity, age, object identity, and MIT-States attributes. Within each regime, we find statistically significant concept directions near-universally across our tested models. However, two distinct regimes do not always share the same concept direction. Several models learn multiple linear structures for the same concept transition, split across regimes. We call this phenomenon "fragmented linearity": strong local linearity coexisting with near-absent global linearity. Fragmentation is, however, not fixed: models with stronger local linearity progressively escape it (local-global linearity correlated with $τ\in [0.38, 0.89]$ across all concepts), and where global linearity does emerge, concept directions can transfer as linear probes across regimes.

others.title: On the stability of learning
others.abstract: Learning algorithms are usually analyzed under the assumption that informative gradients are continuously available. But this is not always true---learning signals in biological neural networks, for example, may be sparse, local, and only intermittently available at any given synapse. In this work, we show that if gradient information is noisy and only intermittently available, learning may be unstable. In particular, even if average learning dynamics converge to the correct optimum, variance in learning may be asymptotically infinite. We explore this point in a number of analytically tractable settings, including single-layer and multi-layer linear networks, and derive explicit conditions under which learning is stable. These conditions complement, but are conceptually distinct from, existing conditions related to the stability of stochastic gradient descent. Our work demonstrates that unbiased credit assignment is not enough for reliable learning; sufficiently frequent and informative feedback is also required, which yields an additional constraint on models of biologically plausible learning.

others.title: FL4N: Feed-forward Latent Model for 4D Novel View Synthesis
others.abstract: 4D novel view synthesis (NVS) aims to render dynamic scenes across viewpoints and timestamps, which requires jointly inferring 3D structure and temporal dynamics. Existing monocular feed-forward methods often rely on explicit 4D Gaussian representations, which are prone to temporal inconsistency and severe rendering artifacts. We present FL4N, the first feed-forward latent 4D NVS model. Instead of relying on explicit 4D primitives, FL4N encodes a 4D scene prior into a unified latent representation across space and time. Our core insight is that learning temporal dynamics as residuals on top of a pretrained static latent prior enables effective 4D modeling with limited dynamic training data. To this end, we introduce a lightweight dynamic encoder that leverages static scene features to disentangle object motion from camera-induced parallax. Trained solely with an image synthesis objective, FL4N achieves state-of-the-art 4D NVS quality while rendering in real time. Its learned latent representation generalizes to real-world videos and disentangles viewpoint from time.
